newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian local polls run smoothly, West watches.
newsitem.headline: Albanian local polls run smoothly, West watches.

text.p: Albanians returned to the polls on Sunday to vote in local ballots five months after a disputed general election with the Central Elections Commission keen to avoid any controversy this time around.
Some 2.2 million Albanians were eligible to take part in the ballot, regarded by the West as a test of the Balkan nation's commitment to democracy.
"There have been no great conflicts. Voting has been calm and some small problems have been cleared up," Central Elections Commission secretary Fiqiri Kupe told Radio Tirana.

Most opposition parties, including the key Socialists, boycotted parliamentary elections in May and June, alleging vote rigging and intimidation by the ruling Democratic Party -- charges upheld by some international observers.

On Sunday, however, the organisers insisted that local ballots were running smoothly with a turnout of around 55 percent by mid-afternoon. They played down reports of ballot irregularities and tensions in some villages.
"The Central Elections Commission has received some reports of irregularities from party sources and it is undertaking some measures to eliminate and clarify them," local news agency ATA reported.

Most ordinary Albanians said they were taking the vote in their stride. "Everything was calm and the situation stable but not so many people were at the polling station," said Zoi, a retired man living in the capital.

The United States and the European Union have sent a clear signal to President Sali Berisha's conservative government that they will watch the local polls closely for signs that Albania is conforming to democratic norms.
The Central Elections Commission has authorised 365 international observers to monitor the vote, according to ATA.
The Council of Europe, which is responsible for coordinating international observers, praised the level of technical cooperation it had received and said it hoped the elections would run smoothly.
President Berisha, a heart surgeon turned politician, declared the local polls would "definitely be free and fair" as he cast his vote near his Tirana apartment.

Polls were to close at nine p.m. (1900 GMT) and final results were expected before the middle of the week. Candidates from 26 parties were fighting for influence in 64 town councils, 36 district councils and 310 communes.

In the last local polls in July 1992, the Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists, won more town halls than the Democrats but the governing party took all the big cities, including Tirana, Durres, Shkoder, Fier and Vlore.
The Democrats also won 43.5 percent of district councils to the Socialists' 41 percent, but the latter got slightly more support in the communal vote.
